text: Pulled the splits from the last five editions. The winning time has moved by 40 seconds total in ten years, but the 100th-place time is four minutes faster. The depth changed, the front didn't.
label: analysis
why: Two checkable numbers, and the contrast between them IS the claim.

text: I tracked sleep against session quality for eleven weeks. Under seven hours the next day's intervals were 6-8 seconds per mile slower, every time bar one. Small sample, one runner, but it's consistent enough that I've stopped scheduling hard days after late shifts.
label: analysis
why: Personal data, stated with its own limits, and the numbers drive the conclusion.

text: The club championship scoring changed in 2019 from top-6 to top-10. Since then our B team has finished above the A team twice. That's not depth improving, it's the scoring rewarding turnout.
label: analysis
why: Named date, named rule change, named consequence.

text: Everyone blames the hill at 18 miles. I split the field into people who ran the first half under 1:45 and over, and the slowdown after 18 was almost identical for both groups. If the hill were the problem the fast starters would fall apart harder.
label: analysis
why: Sets up a test, reports what it showed, draws the inference.

text: Carbon plates aren't the whole story. My times dropped 2% in the shoes and another 2% the following year in the same pair, when the only thing that changed was going from 35 to 50 miles a week.
label: analysis
why: HARD. Reads like a hot take about shoes for one clause, then the second sentence does the work with two comparable numbers. Rule 1: fact carries it.

text: Checked the entry lists. 41% of this year's field have never run the distance before, against 26% five years ago. That's why the finish-line photos look different, not because standards dropped.
label: analysis
why: Two percentages, explicitly used to reject a rival explanation.

text: Ran the same loop in 4C and in 24C within a fortnight, same effort by heart rate. 90 seconds slower in the heat over six miles. People keep saying heat costs you 'a bit' and it's more than that.
label: analysis
why: Controlled-ish comparison with a number attached.

text: Went back through the club results going back to 2012. Every single year the number of people who enter the spring marathon and don't start it sits between 18 and 23 percent. It's not a bad-luck year, it's the base rate.
label: analysis
why: Range across a named span, used to argue against a one-off explanation.

text: The 10K route was remeasured in 2021 and came out 60 metres long. Everyone comparing PBs from before and after that is comparing two different races, which is about 12 seconds at club pace.
label: analysis
why: Date, measurement, and the arithmetic consequence.

text: Three of us ran the same session on the same day, different shoes, within 10 seconds of each other over 5 miles. I'm not saying shoes do nothing, but whatever they do was smaller than the noise between three people.
label: analysis
why: HARD. Hedged conclusion, tiny sample, but the observation is checkable and it is what the claim rests on.

text: Anyone who races more than once a month isn't training, they're just collecting medals.
label: hot_take
why: Assertion about a group, zero support.

text: Heart rate zones are astrology for runners.
label: hot_take
why: Pure claim, and a funny one, but nothing is argued.

text: The club needs to stop pretending the Tuesday session is for everyone. It isn't and it never has been.
label: hot_take
why: Strong, general, unsupported.

text: Times are down about 3% since the shoe rules changed, so obviously the shoes are the whole story and the sport has a problem.
label: hot_take
why: HARD, and the canonical rule-1 case. The 3% is decoration on a conclusion already reached — 'so obviously' does the work, not the number.

text: Marathon training plans are all the same plan with different fonts.
label: hot_take
why: Aphorism, no support offered.

text: If you need a gel before 90 minutes you have a fuelling problem, not an energy problem.
label: hot_take
why: Confident prescription with nothing behind it.

text: Road racing peaked in about 2015 and everything since has been marketing.
label: hot_take
why: Named year, but nothing checkable is offered — the year is part of the assertion, not evidence for it.

text: Track sessions are wasted on anyone running slower than 8 minute miles. You'd get more out of just running more.
label: hot_take
why: Two claims, no support.

text: Nobody actually enjoys the long run. They enjoy having done it, which is a completely different thing, and the sport would be more honest if it said so.
label: hot_take
why: HARD. Reads reflective and almost like reaction, but it is a general claim about everyone rather than a report of the writer's morning. Rule 2.

text: Every injury thread on this forum is the same injury and the same three replies.
label: hot_take
why: HARD. Sounds observational and could be checked in principle, but no count is given — the writer is asserting, not showing.

text: Four minutes off. FOUR. I've been chasing that time for two years and I'm sat on the kerb outside the finish just grinning at nothing.
label: reaction
why: The writer's own race, minutes ago, feeling front and centre. The number is the news, not an argument.

text: Got up at 5, drove ninety minutes, and it's cancelled. Standing in the car park in the rain reading the email.
label: reaction
why: Immediate personal experience.

text: First run back after eight weeks out. Two miles, slower than my warm-up used to be, and I don't care even slightly.
label: reaction
why: Just happened, about the writer, feeling.

text: Watching the last 400 of that and I had to stand up. Still standing up actually.
label: reaction
why: Response to something happening now.

text: Blew up at 20 with the pace band still in my hand like it was going to help. Rough one.
label: reaction
why: Immediate, personal, no general claim.

text: Someone handed my kid an orange slice at mile 22 and I have been crying on and off since.
label: reaction
why: Feeling, immediate, specific to the writer.

text: Wind was so bad on the out section I was leaning at about 20 degrees. Coming back felt like cheating.
label: reaction
why: Report of the run just done.

text: Third DNF this year. I don't really want to talk about it, just wanted to put it somewhere.
label: reaction
why: HARD. 'Third this year' is countable, but nothing is argued from it — it is the writer reporting their own state. Rule 3 doesn't rescue it into analysis because no fact is load-bearing.

text: Just realised the shoes I set every PB in this year are the ones I bought by accident in the wrong size.
label: reaction
why: HARD. A shoe observation, and it could be read as a wry hot take about shoe discourse — but it reports the writer's own realisation, now. Rule 2.

text: Signed up. Card's charged, no going back, immediately regret everything.
label: reaction
why: Immediate, personal, feeling.
